title: What's the difference between a serviced apartment and a condo?
excerpt: They look alike, but serviced apartments sit on commercial land and condos on residential land. Sean explains how that changes car parks, density and utility bills.

question.context: As city land gets more expensive, younger buyers turn to high-rises, and many can't tell a serviced apartment from a condominium.
question.text: How do serviced apartments and condominiums differ, and does it matter to a buyer?

answer.quote: service apartments are constructed on a commercial piece of land
answer.summary: The difference starts with the land: serviced apartments are built on commercial land and condos on residential land. That means serviced apartments may have fewer car parks per unit, far higher density, and commercial utility rates.

reasons.title: Fewer car parks
reasons.body: A serviced apartment needs about 1.5 car parks per unit, a condo two. Fewer bays mean more profit, which is why developers swung to serviced apartments.

reasons.title: Higher density
reasons.body: Condos come with a minimum land size of about three acres and required facilities. Serviced apartments have no such rule, so one acre can hold a few hundred units.

reasons.title: Commercial utility rates
reasons.body: Serviced apartments are billed at commercial rates, though once residents show the building is used as homes, they can appeal to switch to residential rates.

actions: Check whether a project is on commercial or residential title.
Ask how many car parks come with each unit.
Compare the number of units with the land size.
Ask whether residents have switched to residential utility rates.
caveat: These are the planning rules as Sean described them; requirements vary by local authority and may have changed.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for this short video. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased.
